instructions: The night before, or at least 8 hours ahead: put the 1/4 cup soy sauce, 1/4 cup mirin, 1/4 cup sake and 1 tsp sugar in a small saucepan off the heat and whisk until the sugar dissolves.
Bring it to a boil over medium heat, then turn it down and simmer for 1 minute. Take it off the heat and let it cool completely.
Meanwhile, bring 4 cups of water to a full boil in a medium saucepan over high heat. Fill a bowl with ice and cold water.
Lower the eggs into the boiling water one at a time with a slotted spoon, straight from the fridge. Turn the heat down so the water simmers gently and cook them for 7 minutes.
Lift the eggs into the ice water and leave them for 15 minutes, until they're cold all the way through.
Crack the wide end of each egg on the counter and peel the shell off, dipping the egg back in the water if the shell sticks.

Put the peeled eggs in a zip top bag and pour in the cooled marinade. Press out the air and seal it so the eggs sit under the liquid. Put the bag in a bowl in the fridge for 8 hours or overnight, and no longer than a day, or they get too salty.
Take the eggs out of the marinade and cut them in half lengthwise. Serve them cold.
They keep in the fridge for 3 to 4 days in a sealed container. Throw the used marinade away.
advance_prep_notes: Boil the eggs and marinate them overnight, the night before (at least 8 hours).
method_notes: Both read versions simmer soy sauce, mirin, sugar and sake briefly and cool it, boil chilled eggs for a jammy yolk, chill them in iced water, peel them and marinate them in a sealed bag in the fridge overnight. Just One Cookbook (the lead) uses equal parts soy, mirin and sake with a teaspoon of sugar, boils the eggs for 7 minutes and warns against marinating past a day. RecipeTin Japan adds water and bonito flakes to a sweeter marinade, boils them for 6 1/2 minutes and turns them halfway. This follows Just One Cookbook's ratios and its 3 to 4 day keeping time.
